I examine the bar closely. The rust flakes off under my fingers as I run them along its length. This will weaken it more quickly than Mara Voss does during her rounds without notice, but the warden might still detect the difference.

Warden Croft says: "Ah, the infamous Mara Voss, studying her probable exit like a general her battle map."
Warden suspicion is now at 15.
Bar integrity is now at 90.

I examine the bar carefully. I don't want to alert Warden Croft until it's clear whether the window is an escape route or not.

The iron rod feels solid under my fingers, but years of prison routine have made me patient and thorough in my observations. I look for signs of weakness, spots where rust has eaten away at the metal the most. The bars are old, likely as original to this cellblock as the stones that support them, and that's good—for decades of wear and tear implies a structure that has stood up to escape attempts by previous inmates.

Starting at one end, I follow each bar with my gaze, letting the light from the corridor catch the edges. Small imperfections in the metal become visible under my intense scrutiny—flakes of rust here, a tiny crack there. The window bars are set into the stone wall about two feet from the floor and about six inches apart from one another. I can just barely reach the bottom bar with flattened fingers.

As I continue to examine the integrity of the bars themselves, I'm also acutely aware of their placement relative to each other. If two adjacent bars are weak enough, it might serve my purpose better to focus on a different section altogether—or perhaps, if one bar is considerably more worn than its neighbors, concentrating my efforts there could yield quicker results.

This cell is the only home I've had for three years now, and I know every inch of it by heart. The cot frame with its aging paint flakes calls to me from across the room—it has been a while since I tested its sturdiness, after all. Even the loose floor tile has long ago yielded its secrets, but there is comfort in the familiar, an occupational hazard of prolonged incarceration.

I run my fingers along the underside of the bottom bar again, feeling for any signs of weakness. The rust here seems to be less pronounced than further up; perhaps that means this section has been less disturbed—or more? I try to remember how long it's been since I last escaped through these bars. Three years is a long time in the life of a prison; things can change.

Now, if I recall correctly, there was once a small pouch hidden behind one of the stones... but where did I put it after my last escape?

I test the bar with two firm pushes near the bottom, trying to gauge its strength. The rusty metal groans slightly as I press against it.

```
I examine the bar closely. The flakes of rust adhere to my fingertips as I test its thickness near the bottom, where it is set in old mortar that has crumbled away from the surrounding stones over decades of neglect and damp weather that never seems to let these cells dry out completely. It feels fragile at my touch, almost like the rust is a skin over something far more brittle beneath - the iron itself may have eroded away to a point where even an experienced criminal could snap it with a few well placed strikes from a makeshift tool.

As I study the bar for any weaknesses that would make it an easy target for my current needs, I run through the mental checklist I've built up over years of careful observation and patient testing: Rust buildup seems good at this end; any damage done to it will be noticed quickly by Warden Croft, given her habit of scrutinizing the bars every time she enters or leaves a cell, so I'll need to choose my tools wisely. The mortar around here is far too soft for reliable anchoring, but those two cracks above look promising-if only there was some kind of leverage available... Hmm.
```

I examine the bar closely with a practiced eye. Traces on its surface tell me how it was made, what materials were used, where its weak points are likely to be.
A metal implement like this is only so strong as its rivets and its material -- if I can learn its weaknesses, I might find a way it could give out under the right pressure.

This one has been here for years; I have had weeks of idle observation on which to weigh each scratch and twist. The edges are rounded by time and use; the center is almost worn smooth where the wardens' keys have hit it again and again.
I reach out to test whether my observations were accurate, and find that a small amount of rust flakes off beneath my touch. Interesting.

The bar itself remains in as good repair as before. As I draw back, I consider how well its integrity has held up over the course of all this time here. The cell hasn't been improved with it present; no one has come along to replace a better one instead or make a note about needing to reinforce the locks against such a threat.
From any angle the bar looks as if it ought to have lasted many more decades in its current state, given the rest of the cell's upkeep.

Warden suspicion is at an all-time low. Mara Voss hasn't even been in this cell for three days yet; by all accounts she should be the docile, well-behaved prisoner, but I never trust a new one until I've seen her try to escape twice and fail once from trying something clever.

I make a note of my findings about the bar's present state before turning my attention to other parts of the cell. Mara Voss seems to have chosen a good one this time; its last few residents were all small-fry, and no one with real skills for getting out has been in here since the wardens started using this level.
The cell is old -- older than most in this wing -- but it was built solidly enough that age alone didn't give any obvious advantages to an escape attempt. I'll have to examine all of its features closely before I can be sure there are no weak points Mara Voss can exploit.

For now, the bar remains secure as ever.

I examine the bar with a critical eye as I run my hand along its rusted length. The metal creaks slightly under my touch but holds fast. Satisfied that it's not quite ready, I shift my attention to the door instead. I crouch low to the ground and scrutinize the lock on the cell's heavy door, studying the locking mechanism with a trained eye. The keyhole is clogged with dirt and grime from years of neglect—an encouraging sign of a poorly-maintained prison.

As I examine the lock, I speak up. "This place has gone to rot. Even a child could pick that with enough time."

I take the dented aluminium spoon from where it's hidden behind the stack of magazines at the side of my cot and I begin to work on one of the vertical bars of the window frame. The one slightly loose for months now. Bit by bit, with the spoon's edge and a bit of brute force, I try to widen the gap just enough so an adult could pass through it. Then I hide the spoon again, careful not to make any noise or leave traces of my work behind.
The goal is to get Croft off guard while they are busy, so I can escape without them realizing what happened until later, if at all possible. So for now, during this critical phase, I try to keep a low profile and stay as unnoticed by them as possible.
With a spoon in hand it'll take me around two weeks to make the window passable. But I have no other option right now. And time is precious. Every day closer to the day they're transferring me to another block, my chances of success diminish dramatically. The risk might be high, but what does one have to lose if the alternative is a life in a small cell? So I continue my work in silence and with great care and patience. Day by day I get a bit further until eventually, the window is passable. Until then, I keep low profile and behave as usual during the daily rounds of Croft, so his suspicion will not rise prematurely.

I pull the bar towards myself with a low groan as if testing its strength. "Huhl, rusty," I murmur, letting go. The sound echoes in the cell.

I examine the bar closely, running my fingers across its surface. The rust flakes off in places, showing glimpses of the iron beneath. I try to gauge how much time I'd have if I were to attempt an escape this way, but Croft is watching me like a hawk - there'll be no simple solution here.

As I study the bar, I speak up, "You've had me in here for three years now, Warden Croft. You must know by now I'm not going anywhere until you let me."

The cell feels colder than usual today, and the air is heavy with the weight of Croft's presence. The spoon, I think to myself, might just be my ticket out of here if I can weaken it enough. But I'll need to work on it unseen - a tricky task given how closely Croft inspects everything in this room.

For now though, I continue to examine the bar, running my fingers over its surface and testing its strength with subtle pressure. If I can find even the slightest weakness, some way to subtly damage it further without drawing too much attention... but Croft is no fool, and I'll need to be careful if I want this escape attempt to pay off.

```
I examine the bar closely with my hand. The rust flakes off under my fingers, a few black grains falling to the floor, and I judge it weak about halfway up from its base in the wall.

Warden Croft eyes me carefully, arms crossed to rest on his belly, the keys jangling slightly by his leg as he shifts his foot.
"Keep your hands where I can see them, Voss." 
He leans forward a bit, peering down at my fidgeting fingers. "Don't go thinking you've been here long enough for these bars to rot through on their own."
The bar doesn't look it, but with the right tool and some time, I think it could be done without too much noise. Quieter than the lock, at least.

What I don't say is how my shoulders ache from working at that point every night under cover of the bucket hitting the floor when they slide the tray through. How each flake rust has a name and a number of days attached to it in my mind. How I remember where it is weakest now, and which direction it must be bent for the old mortar to crumble faster.
What he doesn't know is that I've had practice. And that the next bar over isn't my only target this time.

I work my jaw a bit and then say, "Old bars are just dry, is all. You don't have to watch so closely, Croft." A beat of quiet, nothing but the sound of the wind moaning somewhere in the distance. Then I go back to working at the lock with that little nail file they slipped me last time I was up for visitation.

What I'm doing this round is seeing if I can get a look at what your cell and the game are like after you've been playing a while, Voss. Not much has changed so far, but you never know when some detail will give you that little more insight into how Croft ticks or what they might be carrying of interest. You work on that bar slowly, carefully, in small increments lest their eyes find the wrong place and zero suspicion is lost to a single outburst. It's all about subtlety, patience, and an eye for the details others would miss.
```

```
I examine the bar with a critical eye. The rust flakes off under my finger, and I can see where the iron is beginning to give way from repeated stress testing over weeks and months. I make a note on my clipboard.

The spoon catches my attention next. It's one of those aluminum jobs, thin enough that if a prisoner wanted to they could probably bend it into a makeshift tool or weapon with some time and patience... assuming the warden wasn't keeping close watch, checking for any signs of "excessive interest".

My eyes drift up towards the window, where that bar is set into place. That's the real prize, if Mara can get her hands on that without my noticing... I'd have no choice but to turn this cell into a maximum-security holding until we could replace it with something sturdier.

I pace around the room in a slow circle, considering each point of potential Weakness while trying not to let my gaze linger too long any one spot. Mara's watching me like a hawk, I can tell She's waiting for an opening and I don't intend to give Her one if I can help it.
```
